idiom_name: Diesel .for_update() (PostgreSQL/MySQL) or a raw SELECT ... FOR UPDATE through sqlx
implementation_notes: Diesel's query DSL exposes for_update(), for_no_key_update(), for_share(), skip_locked() and no_wait(), documented as available for MySQL and PostgreSQL only; a SQLite-backed service cannot express a row lock and must use BEGIN IMMEDIATE, while sqlx has no builder for it, so sqlx users send the SELECT ... FOR UPDATE text themselves. In every case the lock ends at commit and the offline lease is a lock record with owner and timeout, so the classic lock-manager structure is what makes the primitive an offline lock.
pitfalls: for_update() only compiles for backends implementing LockingDsl (MySQL/PostgreSQL); on SQLite the code fails to compile, so a dialect-agnostic service must hide the lock behind a trait or raw SQL.
Diesel connections are synchronous: taking a blocking lock inside a tokio task without spawn_blocking stalls the executor.
Waiting on a row lock can outlive the request timeout; prefer no_wait()/skip_locked() and return 'locked by X' immediately.
